stories.headline: How India Avoided An LPG Shortage Amid West Asia War | Hardeep Singh Puri
stories.title: How India Avoided An LPG Shortage Amid West Asia War | Hardeep Singh Puri
stories.summary: Union Petroleum and Natural Gas Minister Hardeep Singh Puri has explained how India managed its energy supplies amid global geopolitical tensions and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. Puri said India had approximately 60 days of crude oil and natural gas supplies even under an extreme disruption scenario. However, LPG remained a concern because three major suppliers – Qatar, the UAE and Saudi Arabia – are located near the Strait of Hormuz. To strengthen domestic availability, India ramped up daily LPG production from around 35,000 metric tonnes to 55,000 metric tonnes. Puri credited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership and cooperation between public and private sector companies, claiming that not one of India's 1.07 lakh retail outlets ran dry.

stories.title: Cyclone Akvan: Odisha evacuates over 300K people, 47 trains cancelled
stories.summary: Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi said preparations were under way across 20 districts to meet the zero-casualty target, with 4,170 pregnant women shifted to safe shelters ahead of landfall
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Odisha is on high alert as Cyclone Akvan approaches, with 47 trains cancelled, 28 rescheduled and schools shut in nine districts.
More than three lakh people have been evacuated, while airlines issue travel advisories and rescue teams prepare for the storm.
Cyclone Akvan has prompted extensive precautionary measures across Odisha, disrupting rail and air travel and forcing schools in nine districts to close.
More than three lakh people have been evacuated, while rescue teams and cyclone shelters have been placed on alert ahead of the storm's expected landfall near Gopalpur.

Odisha has stepped up its cyclone preparedness as Cyclone Akvan approaches the eastern coast, with transport services disrupted, schools closed in vulnerable districts and large-scale evacuations underway.
Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi reviewed the state's preparedness on Thursday and said more than three lakh people had been moved to safer locations.
According to an official release, the administration is coordinating with district authorities and central government departments to minimise casualties and protect people in vulnerable areas.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast that the cyclone is likely to cross the North Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and South Odisha coasts near Gopalpur on Friday afternoon.
Railway services have been affected as a precaution against the expected weather conditions.
Chief Minister Majhi said 47 trains had been cancelled and 28 rescheduled.
The cancellations include long-distance express services, Vande Bharat trains, passenger services and MEMU trains.
Passengers travelling through Puri, Bhubaneswar, Cuttack and Berhampur may face disruptions.

stories.headline: Cyclone Akvan: Light rain in parts of Jharkhand; primary classes suspended in some districts
stories.title: Cyclone Akvan: Light rain in parts of Jharkhand; primary classes suspended in some districts
stories.summary: East Singhbhum and Saraikela-Kharswan district administrations have ordered schools to suspend primary classes on Friday (November 20, 2026) in view of the cyclone
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Parts of Jharkhand experienced light rainfall on Friday (November 20, 2026) morning under the influence of Cyclone Akvan as some district authorities suspended primary classes in schools, an official said.
The landfall process of the cyclone commenced near Gopalpur in Odisha around 8 a.m.

Rainfall is expected to intensify in the afternoon, as the IMD has issued an 'orange' alert (be prepared) for heavy downpour in five Jharkhand districts till 8.30 a.m. on Saturday (November 21, 2026), the official said.
East Singhbhum and Saraikela-Kharswan district administrations have ordered schools to suspend primary classes on Friday (November 20, 2026) in view of the cyclone.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued an 'orange' alert for heavy rainfall in Dhanbad, Bokaro, Seraikela-Kharswan, and East and West Singhbhum districts till 8.30 a.m. on Saturday (November 21, 2026).
A 'yellow' alert (be updated) for heavy rain has been issued for Lohardaga, Gumla, Simdega, Ranchi, Khunti, Ramgarh and Jamtara for the same period, a weather bulletin said.
"The rainfall is likely to intensify later in the day and some districts may experience very heavy rainfall.
Thunderstorms accompanied by lightning are also likely in some places along with gusty winds of up to 50 kmph speed," Ranchi Meteorological Centre Deputy Director Abhishek Anand said.
He said the situation is expected to improve from November 22 and clear skies are likely from November 23.

stories.headline: What Trump's meetings in Asia reveal
stories.title: What Trump's meetings in Asia reveal
stories.summary: Washington: US President Donald Trump huddled with leaders from longtime partners Japan, Australia and India in a resort conference room in Manila, Philippines, this week to strengthen a partnership called the Quad that is meant to counter China.Two days later, Trump warmly greeted Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in an unprecedented, trilateral summit of countries that have been long considered rivals to take on "new opportunities and approaches on a range of very important issues".Trump effusively described all these leaders as friends, but the meetings highlighted some key differences. The two geopolitical gatherings on the same whirlwind Asia trip reflect the US president's varied foreign policy approaches at a time when the world order is shifting."The Quad, comprising four democracies that uphold the rule of law, represents the post-World War II international order," said Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow focused on Asia at the Hudson Institute."The trilateral, meanwhile, raises the prospect of a very different order -- one in which three great powers stand above the rest, recognise each other's spheres of influence and refrain from interfering in each other's core interests." The Quad meeting was a much different scene than Trump-Xi-Putin summitIn a no-frills hotel conference room in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, Trump sat down with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.Covered in blue cloth, four long tables formed the appropriate shape of a quadrilateral, with each government taking one side. The leaders were flanked by their Cabinet members. There were no decorations but a mandatory display of national flags.Before the meeting, the four leaders took a photo together, where Trump took questions from reporters and joked around with his counterparts.Calling the leaders "friends of mine", Trump turned to Albanese and patted him on the back, as the Australian premier nodded. Trump then threw his thumb towards Modi and joked, "And by the way, he's a very tough man," before pointing to Takaichi and saying, "and she may be even tougher".Modi didn't crack a smile, but Takaichi chuckled. Trump turned back to Albanese: "And we? We're OK, too," to which the Australian laughed.Moments earlier, Modi, apparently impatient, gestured to end the press conference to no avail as Trump kept taking questions.The scene was much grander but far less spontaneous two days later when Trump joined Putin and Xi at a massive ring-shaped table with a burst of pink flowers in the middle at a state-owned resort in Shenzhen, China. The room was spacious with marble flooring, crystal chandeliers and jade sculptures.Three leaders were alone at the table, seated some distance from one another. Xi read from a prepared script, with hardly any expression on his face. Putin looked at the documents in front of him, while Trump sat back with a slight smile on the opposite end of the table. Trump says he's friends with everyone In Manila, Trump said at the Quad meeting that "we're all friends" and suggested that the leaders from Japan, Australia and India can reach him directly."We talk a lot when they have a problem, when they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open and the Oval Office is always open to you," Trump said.Talking to reporters, Trump praised his fellow Quad leaders, calling them "phenomenal people"."And they're friends of mine, so that helps," the US president said.On Thursday, Trump described Xi and Putin similarly, addressing both as his "friend". At the airport in Shenzhen, Trump got a rare greeting there from Xi and even an unusual hug from the Chinese leader.At a welcoming ceremony for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation grouping, Putin joined Xi and Trump on stage. He and Trump shook hands and held each other briefly by the arm, with Xi looking on and smiling.At the trilateral meeting, Trump argued that differences among countries should not forestall talks. "Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And, uh, we feel the opposite," Trump said. The statements from the two meetings diverge The joint press release from the Quad leaders called the group "a force for good and a partnership of action, committed to peace, stability, and prosperity" and laid out areas for cooperation, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and maritime surveillance.The Chinese, US and Russian governments issued a statement committing to reforming the United Nations, planning to increase petroleum supplies and affirming opposition to nuclear wars.While the Quad statement was substantive and reflective of the alignment of the four nations, the trilateral statement was largely symbolic. Still, it offered more detail than expected, said Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia.With language about nuclear weapons and future dialogue, "it is a major concession by China," said Kagan, now a senior advisor at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The trilateral, meanwhile, raises the prospect of a very different order -- one in which three great powers stand above the rest, recognise each other's spheres of influence and refrain from interfering in each other's core interests." The Quad meeting was a much different scene than Trump-Xi-Putin summit.

In a no-frills hotel conference room in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, Trump sat down with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
Covered in blue cloth, four long tables formed the appropriate shape of a quadrilateral, with each government taking one side.
The leaders were flanked by their Cabinet members.
There were no decorations but a mandatory display of national flags.
Before the meeting, the four leaders took a photo together, where Trump took questions from reporters and joked around with his counterparts.
Calling the leaders "friends of mine", Trump turned to Albanese and patted him on the back, as the Australian premier nodded.
Trump then threw his thumb towards Modi and joked, "And by the way, he's a very tough man," before pointing to Takaichi and saying, "and she may be even tougher".
Modi didn't crack a smile, but Takaichi chuckled.
Trump turned back to Albanese: "And we?
We're OK, too," to which the Australian laughed.
Moments earlier, Modi, apparently impatient, gestured to end the press conference to no avail as Trump kept taking questions.

The scene was much grander but far less spontaneous two days later when Trump joined Putin and Xi at a massive ring-shaped table with a burst of pink flowers in the middle at a state-owned resort in Shenzhen, China.
The room was spacious with marble flooring, crystal chandeliers and jade sculptures.
Three leaders were alone at the table, seated some distance from one another.
Xi read from a prepared script, with hardly any expression on his face.
Putin looked at the documents in front of him, while Trump sat back with a slight smile on the opposite end of the table.
Trump says he's friends with everyone.

In Manila, Trump said at the Quad meeting that "we're all friends" and suggested that the leaders from Japan, Australia and India can reach him directly." We talk a lot when they have a problem, when they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open and the Oval Office is always open to you," Trump said.
Talking to reporters, Trump praised his fellow Quad leaders, calling them "phenomenal people"." And they're friends of mine, so that helps," the US president said.
On Thursday, Trump described Xi and Putin similarly, addressing both as his "friend".
At the airport in Shenzhen, Trump got a rare greeting there from Xi and even an unusual hug from the Chinese leader.
At a welcoming ceremony for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation grouping, Putin joined Xi and Trump on stage.
He and Trump shook hands and held each other briefly by the arm, with Xi looking on and smiling.
At the trilateral meeting, Trump argued that differences among countries should not forestall talks.
"Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements.
And, uh, we feel the opposite," Trump said.
The statements from the two meetings diverge.

The joint press release from the Quad leaders called the group "a force for good and a partnership of action, committed to peace, stability, and prosperity" and laid out areas for cooperation, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and maritime surveillance.
The Chinese, US and Russian governments issued a statement committing to reforming the United Nations, planning to increase petroleum supplies and affirming opposition to nuclear wars.
While the Quad statement was substantive and reflective of the alignment of the four nations, the trilateral statement was largely symbolic.
Still, it offered more detail than expected, said Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia.
With language about nuclear weapons and future dialogue, "it is a major concession by China," said Kagan, now a senior advisor at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
